reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A tauopathy presenting with markedly asymmetric parkinsonism combined with cortical signs, poorly responsive to levodopa
The alien limb phenomenon, in which a limb moves or interferes without volitional control, is a striking but not invariable feature
Cortical sensory loss, apraxia, and focal dystonia or myoclonus of the affected limb are characteristic
Rigidity and bradykinesia are typically one-sided at onset before spreading
Cognitive and language impairment, including a nonfluent aphasia, may dominate in some patients
The clinical picture (corticobasal syndrome) can be produced by several pathologies, so clinical and pathological diagnoses do not always match
MRI often shows asymmetric cortical atrophy, typically greatest in the frontoparietal regions opposite the affected side
Distinguishing features from Parkinson disease include marked asymmetry, cortical signs, and poor levodopa response
reference.pathophysiology: Corticobasal degeneration is a four-repeat tauopathy with neuronal and glial tau deposition, including astrocytic plaques, and ballooned achromatic neurons, affecting the cerebral cortex (especially frontoparietal) and the basal ganglia asymmetrically. Cortical involvement produces apraxia, cortical sensory loss, and the alien limb phenomenon, while basal ganglia and nigral degeneration cause the akinetic-rigid, dystonic parkinsonism. Because the corticobasal syndrome can arise from Alzheimer, progressive supranuclear palsy, or other pathologies, the underlying substrate is confirmed only at autopsy.
additionalDifferentials: Alzheimer disease (which can present as corticobasal syndrome)
Frontotemporal dementia and primary progressive aphasia
Focal structural lesions or vascular parkinsonism
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain to demonstrate asymmetric frontoparietal atrophy and exclude structural lesions
Neuropsychological testing to characterise apraxia, cortical sensory loss, and language impairment
Trial of dopaminergic therapy to document limited benefit
Biomarkers for Alzheimer pathology when it is a plausible underlying cause
Functional imaging (e.g. FDG-PET) showing asymmetric hypometabolism in selected cases
redFlags: Rapid cognitive decline affecting safety, decision-making, and capacity
Severe apraxia or dystonia causing loss of limb function and falls
Features pointing to a potentially treatable alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The disorder is progressive and untreatable at its root, with worsening motor disability, apraxia, and cognition over several years; survival typically spans several years from diagnosis, with aspiration and immobility complications determining outcome.
pitfalls: Labeling asymmetric parkinsonism as Parkinson disease and persisting with ineffective levodopa
Equating the corticobasal syndrome with corticobasal degeneration pathology, which often differs
Overlooking cortical signs such as apraxia and cortical sensory loss
Missing an underlying Alzheimer pathology that alters counselling and management
Attributing the alien limb or dystonia to a functional or psychiatric cause
